title: The “Still True?” Practice for a Changing Day
markdown:
# The “Still True?” Practice for a Changing Day

Some thoughts arrive with the force of a verdict: this is too much, I always get this wrong, nothing is moving, I cannot settle. In the middle of a difficult moment, the thought may feel permanent simply because it is present.

The “Still True?” practice is a short way to meet that feeling without arguing with yourself or trying to replace it with a better one. Its purpose is to notice what has changed inside a situation that seems fixed. You can use it after an upsetting conversation, during an ordinary low spell, or when your mind has been circling one concern for a while.

The central question is simple: **What, if anything, is still true now?**

It does not ask whether your first reaction was wrong. It asks you to return a little later and see whether the whole experience is exactly as it was.

## Set aside six quiet minutes

Choose a moment when you have moved at least slightly away from the event or thought you want to reflect on. You do not need ideal conditions. A chair, a note on your phone, or the edge of a kitchen table is enough.

Begin by naming the moment in one sentence. Keep it concrete.

“I received a message that made me feel dismissed.”

“I looked at my work list and felt behind.”

“I woke up with a heavy mood.”

Then write two brief lines:

- “At first, I believed…”
- “Right now, what is still true is…”

For the first line, let yourself state the original conclusion plainly. Do not edit it into something reasonable. For the second, look for details rather than reassurance. Perhaps the feeling remains, but its intensity has shifted. Perhaps you now know one more piece of information. Perhaps the body is tired while the situation itself is unresolved. Perhaps the mind is still making a prediction, but you can see it as a prediction rather than a fact.

A useful answer may be very modest: “I am still hurt, but I am no longer shaking.” Or: “The deadline is still close, but I have completed the first task.”

Pause after writing. Take one unforced breath, and read both lines once. The difference between them is the material of the practice.

## Ask three narrowing questions

If the second line feels vague, use these questions one at a time. Write no more than two or three sentences for each.

First ask: **What has changed since the first reaction?**

Look for changes in time, information, surroundings, and body. The change may be small: you drank water, another person replied, the room became quieter, or an hour passed. Small changes matter because they show that the experience is not a single solid block.

Next ask: **What has not changed?**

This keeps the practice honest. You may still need to make a decision, repair a relationship, rest, or finish something. Reflection is not useful when it requires you to deny the part that remains difficult. Naming what persists gives the mind less reason to defend itself.

Finally ask: **What is true only for this moment?**

This question is especially helpful when the mind reaches for words such as always, never, ruined, or impossible. You might write, “At this moment, I do not know how the conversation will go,” rather than “This relationship is ruined.” Or, “At this moment, I do not want to begin,” rather than “I cannot do this.”

The aim is not to make the moment pleasant. It is to give it its proper size.

## An example from an ordinary afternoon

Imagine that you send a piece of work to someone and receive no response for several hours. By late afternoon, you notice yourself checking for messages repeatedly. Your first line might be:

“At first, I believed they were unhappy with what I sent.”

When you return to the practice, you might write:

“Right now, what is still true is that I have not received a reply and I feel uneasy.”

Then the three questions could reveal the following:

“What has changed since the first reaction? I have reread what I sent and noticed it was clear. I also remembered that they often answer later in the day.”

“What has not changed? I still do not know what they think, and I may need to revise the work when they respond.”

“What is true only for this moment? I am waiting, and waiting is uncomfortable.”

Notice that none of these sentences force a positive interpretation. The reply may still contain criticism. But the original conclusion has loosened from certainty into one possible explanation. That shift can make room for the next sensible action: return to another task, make tea, or decide when you will check messages again.

## Close with one sentence for later

End by completing this sentence: **“When this changes again, I want to remember…”**

Keep the answer practical. “My first thought is not my final understanding.” “Waiting feels larger when I keep checking.” “A difficult feeling can remain without explaining everything.”

You can repeat this practice with the same situation later in the day or the next morning. Comparing your notes is optional; the value can also be in returning to the question each time the mind treats a passing state as a permanent description of your life.
